title: Output Contest Matches
statement:
`n` teams are seeded from 1 (strongest) to `n` (weakest), and `n` is a power of two. A knockout bracket is drawn round by round from an ordered list of entries, which starts as the teams `1, 2, ..., n`:

- In each round, the first entry is paired with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on.
- A pair is written `(x,y)`, with the entry that came earlier in the list first. Here `x` and `y` are team numbers or pairs written in an earlier round.
- The pairs, in the order they were formed, become the list for the next round.

When a single entry is left, return it as a string. It contains only digits, parentheses and commas, with no spaces.
constraints: n == 2^k for some integer k with 1 <= k <= 12
notes:
## Intuition

The rules describe a simulation, and simulating them directly is efficient. Keep the current list of entries as strings. One round pairs the entry at index `i` with the entry at the mirrored index `length - 1 - i`, which halves the list. The new list stays ordered from strongest to weakest, because the pair holding the better seed is formed first, so the same rule applies again in the next round. After log₂ n rounds a single string is left.

Another way to get the answer, used by the brute force, is to compute the order in which the teams appear in the final string and then add the brackets recursively.

## Approach

1. Fill `teams` with the strings `"1"` to `"n"`.
2. While more than one entry is left, build `next`: for each `i` in the first half, append `(teams[i],teams[teams.length - 1 - i])`.
3. Replace `teams` with `next`.
4. Return the only remaining entry.

## Example 1, step by step

For `n = 4`, `teams` starts as `["1", "2", "3", "4"]`. Round 1 pairs index 0 with 3 and index 1 with 2, giving `["(1,4)", "(2,3)"]`. Round 2 pairs those two, giving `["((1,4),(2,3))"]`, which is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): there are log₂ n rounds, and each one copies every character built so far, which is O(n) numbers, brackets and commas.
- Space: O(n) for the current list of entries and the final string, counting each team number as one unit.

## Pitfalls

- Pair index `i` with `teams.length - 1 - i`, not with its neighbour `i + 1`; neighbours only meet after the bracket is built.
- Keep `next` in the order the pairs are made. Sorting it, or writing the weaker entry first, changes the answer.
- After round 1 the entries are nested strings, so keep them as text instead of numbers.
- The format has no spaces: `(1,4)`, not `(1, 4)`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `teams` | the entries of the current round, strongest first |
| `next` | the pairs formed in this round, which make up the next round |
| `i` | the index of the stronger entry of the pair being formed |

narration.3: Start with every team as its own entry, seed 1 first.
narration.4: Store team i as text so it can be nested inside brackets later.
narration.6: Keep playing rounds until only one entry remains.
narration.7: Collect the pairs formed in this round.
narration.8: Walk through the stronger half of the list.
narration.9: Pair entry i with its mirror from the end and write the pair as (x,y).
narration.11: The pairs, still strongest first, become the next round's entries.
narration.13: The single remaining entry is the whole bracket.
